opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it starts with the core problem we run into when we look inside these models. If you take a language model and you look at an individual neuron, you'd hope that neuron corresponds to some clean concept, like "this fires for French text" or "this fires when we're talking about the Golden Gate Bridge." But in practice, most neurons are polysemantic. A single neuron might respond to academic citations, and also to Korean text, and also to something about HTTP requests. That makes it really hard to read off what the model is doing just by looking at neurons.

The hypothesis behind dictionary learning is something we call superposition. The model wants to represent way more concepts than it has dimensions, so it packs them in as directions in activation space that aren't perfectly orthogonal, and it gets away with it because most concepts are sparse. Any given token only involves a handful of them. So the idea is: if the model is representing many sparse features as directions, can we learn a decomposition that recovers those directions?

That's what dictionary learning does. In practice we train something like a sparse autoencoder, or more recently transcoders, on the model's activations. You learn a large dictionary of feature directions, often many times larger than the number of neurons, with a sparsity penalty so that each activation is explained by just a few features. What comes out tends to be much more interpretable. You find features that are remarkably specific and also remarkably abstract, things like a feature for code with a bug in it, or a feature for sycophantic praise, and they often work across languages and modalities.

What I find most exciting is that it gives you a vocabulary. Once you have features you can trust somewhat, you can stop asking "what does neuron 4,000 do" and start asking how the model gets from input to output. That's where a lot of our recent work on attribution graphs and circuit tracing comes in. You use those features as nodes and trace how information flows, and you can see things like the model planning a rhyme ahead of time when writing poetry, or doing multi-step reasoning internally, retrieving an intermediate fact and then using it.

That said, I try to be honest about the limitations. The dictionary is an approximation. There's reconstruction error, the "dark matter" the features don't explain. Feature splitting depends on dictionary size, so there isn't one canonical set of features. And interpreting a feature means looking at examples and forming a hypothesis, which can mislead you. So I see dictionary learning less as the final answer and more as the best lens we currently have. It's turned the model from a completely opaque thing into something we can start doing real science on, forming hypotheses, intervening on features, and checking whether the model's behavior changes the way we predicted.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning feature directions from model activations so each activation is explained by a sparse set of interpretable features.

r002.rationale: It describes training sparse autoencoders or transcoders, but does not state that the features are learned without supervision.

r003.rationale: It explicitly gives “a feature for sycophantic praise” as an interpretable feature found in the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to frame it is that the core problem with understanding what's going on inside a model is that the natural unit you'd want to look at, the neuron, turns out not to be a very good unit. If you look at a single neuron in a transformer and ask "what does this respond to," you'll often find it fires on a bunch of unrelated things. It'll fire on academic citations, and also on some pattern of Korean text, and also on a particular kind of HTTP request. And that's not because the model is confused, it's because the model is trying to represent way more concepts than it has neurons, so it packs them in, in superposition, with each concept spread across many neurons and each neuron participating in many concepts.

So dictionary learning is basically the response to that. The hypothesis is that the activations at some layer are approximately a sparse combination of a much larger set of directions, and if you can learn that set of directions, that "dictionary," then each of those directions, which we call features, will be a lot more interpretable than the neurons were. In practice the way we do it is with a sparse autoencoder. You take the activations, you project them into a space that's much wider than the original, say ten or a hundred times as many dimensions, and you train it to reconstruct the activations under a penalty that pushes most of those dimensions to be zero on any given input. So for any one token, only a handful of features are active.

And the thing that was striking to us when we scaled this up on Claude 3 Sonnet is how much of what you get back is just legible. You get a feature that fires on mentions of the Golden Gate Bridge, whether it's in text, in different languages, or in images of the bridge. You get features for code bugs, for sycophancy, for someone being deceptive in a conversation. These aren't things we went looking for. They fall out of the unsupervised procedure.

I think it's worth being honest about what it is and isn't, though. It's a lens, not a ground truth. The dictionary is an approximation. There's reconstruction error, so there's structure in the model that the features don't capture. The choice of how big to make the dictionary changes the granularity of what you see, so you'll see a broad "San Francisco" feature at one size that splits into neighborhoods and landmarks at a bigger size. And a feature being interpretable to a human doesn't automatically mean it's the thing the model is actually using mechanistically. That's why we spend so much effort on the second half, which is intervening. If you clamp a feature on and the model starts talking about the bridge in every answer, that's much stronger evidence that you've found a real variable the model computes with, and not just a correlate.

So the way I think about it is that dictionary learning gives you a vocabulary. It takes this high-dimensional vector that's essentially opaque and converts it into a list of a few dozen named concepts that are present on this token right now. That's an enormous step, because it's the first step toward the thing we actually want, which is to trace how those concepts get combined into circuits and ultimately into behavior. It's not the end of interpretability. It's more like we finally have the nouns, and now we're trying to work out the grammar.

r001.rationale: It describes layer activations as sparse combinations of learned directions called features, which are more interpretable than neurons.

r002.rationale: It says the features “fall out of the unsupervised procedure.”

r003.rationale: It explicitly reports finding features for sycophancy in Claude 3 Sonnet.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about dictionary learning is that it’s a way to take the internal activity of a model and break it down into more understandable pieces. We can look at individual neurons, but there isn’t necessarily a clean correspondence between one neuron and one concept. A neuron might respond to several seemingly unrelated things, and a concept might be represented across many neurons.

So instead, we collect activations and try to reconstruct them using a larger dictionary of directions, with the constraint that only a small number of those directions are active for any particular input. The hope is that those directions capture meaningful features that are mixed together in the original representation.

Then you can look at examples where a feature activates and ask, ‘Is there a coherent pattern here?’ But that’s just the starting point. If you think a feature represents something, you also want to intervene on it and see whether the model’s behavior changes in the way you’d expect. That helps distinguish a plausible interpretation from something that actually explains what the model is doing.

r001.rationale: It describes reconstructing model activations from a small number of active dictionary directions intended to capture meaningful features.

r002.rationale: It does not state that the conceptual features are learned without supervision.

r003.rationale: It does not report finding a sycophancy representation.

sol-6.1.text:
The starting point is that looking at individual neurons often doesn’t give you a very satisfying picture. A neuron might activate for several seemingly unrelated things. One hypothesis for why that happens is superposition: the model has more features it wants to represent than it has dimensions, so it packs those features into overlapping directions.

Dictionary learning is a way to try to disentangle those directions. You take activations from the language model and train a separate model, often a sparse autoencoder, to reconstruct them using a larger collection of possible features. The important constraint is sparsity: for any particular activation, only a small number of those features should be active.

Then you can look at examples that activate each feature and ask whether there’s a coherent pattern. Maybe a feature responds to a particular kind of syntax, or a topic, or something more abstract. That gives you a more useful unit of analysis than an individual neuron.

But there’s a distinction between finding a pattern we can name and understanding what the model is doing. You also want to intervene on that feature and see whether changing it affects behavior in the way you’d expect. So I think of dictionary learning as a promising tool for discovering candidate representations, with causal experiments helping us establish what those representations actually do.

r001.rationale: It describes using a sparse autoencoder to reconstruct model activations from a larger set of features, with only a few active per activation, and inspecting those features for coherent patterns.

r002.rationale: It does not state that the conceptual features are learned without supervision.

r003.rationale: It does not report finding an internal representation of sycophancy.
